title: Keeping Time with the Skies
subject: Science
description: Phases of the Moon and why they happen, locating the Moon, moonrise delay, eclipses and tides, the solar day, lunar/solar/luni-solar calendars, leap years, the Indian National Calendar, Uttarayan and Dakshinayan, festival dates, and artificial satellites launched by ISRO.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: In the chapter's opening story, where was Meera when she noticed the Moon shining in the daytime sky?
options: At the International Kite Festival in Ahmedabad
At the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics in Kolkata
At the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre in Thiruvananthapuram
At the Positional Astronomy Centre in New Delhi
questions.explanation: Meera was in Ahmedabad for the Patang Mahotsav (International Kite Festival) on Makar Sankranti when she saw the Moon during the day. The other places are mentioned elsewhere in the chapter for different reasons.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: The two-week period during which the bright portion of the Moon shrinks from a full circle until it is no longer visible is called the
options: waxing period
waning period
gibbous period
crescent period
questions.explanation: The bright portion decreasing from full to half to invisible over about two weeks is the waning period. Waxing is the opposite (growing); gibbous and crescent are names of shapes, not of periods.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Which Indian name is given to the day when the Moon appears as a full bright circle?
options: Amavasya
Shukla Paksha
Purnima
Krishna Paksha
questions.explanation: Full Moon day is Purnima; Amavasya is the new Moon day when the Moon is not visible. Shukla and Krishna Paksha are the two fortnights (waxing and waning), not single days.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Starting from the full Moon, roughly how long does it take for the bright portion of the Moon to shrink to a half circle?
options: About two weeks
About one month
About three days
About one week
questions.explanation: The text says the bright portion decreases from a full circle to a half circle in about a week, and keeps shrinking for another week until it disappears (two weeks in total for waning).

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: In India, the waxing period of the Moon is generally called the
options: Shukla Paksha
Krishna Paksha
Adhika Maasa
Purnimant month
questions.explanation: Shukla Paksha is the bright/waxing fortnight; Krishna Paksha is the dark/waning fortnight. Adhika Maasa is an extra intercalary month and Purnimant is a type of month-reckoning.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Which sequence correctly lists the Moon's shapes as seen from Earth in the two weeks after a new Moon?
options: Gibbous, half circle, crescent, full Moon
Crescent, half circle, gibbous, full Moon
Full Moon, gibbous, half circle, crescent
Half circle, crescent, gibbous, full Moon
questions.explanation: After new Moon the bright part grows: a thin crescent first, a half circle after about a week, then gibbous (more than half), and a full circle after another week. The reverse order describes waning.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Which statement about the Moon's monthly cycle is NOT correct?
options: A waning period is always followed by a waxing period in a cycle
The cycle from one full Moon to the next takes about a month
The Moon's own shape changes from day to day during the month
After a new Moon the bright part grows to a half circle in about a week
questions.explanation: The Moon's actual shape never changes; only the part of its illuminated half that we can see changes. The other three statements are exactly what the chapter describes.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Krishna Paksha is the fortnight in which the bright portion of the Moon increases every night.
questions.explanation: False. Krishna Paksha is the waning period, when the bright portion decreases. The growing (waxing) fortnight is Shukla Paksha.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: The cycle from one full Moon to the next full Moon takes about a month.
questions.explanation: True. The waning period (about two weeks) followed by the waxing period (about two weeks) brings the Moon back to full in roughly a month.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: According to the chapter, what exactly is meant by the 'phases of the Moon'?
options: The changing distance between the Moon and the Earth during one month
The changing times at which the Moon rises and sets over successive days
The changing shadows that the Earth casts on the Moon during an eclipse
The changing shapes of the Moon's bright portion from day to day as seen from Earth
questions.explanation: Phases are defined as the changing shapes of the bright portion of the Moon from one day to another as seen from Earth. Rising times do change daily, but that is not what 'phases' means, and Earth's shadow causes eclipses, not phases.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Activity 11.1 asks you to watch the Moon at sunrise for about 15 days and then at sunset for the next 15 days. Why is the switch needed?
options: After new Moon the waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset
After full Moon the Moon can be seen only during the daytime
The Moon stops rising in the east after about fifteen days
Sunrise observations are impossible during the waxing fortnight
questions.explanation: The first 15 days after full Moon are the waning period, when the Moon is easiest to see at sunrise. After new Moon it waxes, and a waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset — so the observing time is switched.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: On the first day after the full Moon, in which direction should you look for the Moon at sunrise?
options: Eastern direction
Western direction
Directly overhead
Northern direction
questions.explanation: Just after full Moon the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun, so when the Sun rises in the east the Moon is almost setting in the west.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Select the TWO correct pairings of a term with its meaning.
options: Purnima — the day the Moon is not visible
Shukla Paksha — the waxing period of the Moon
Amavasya — the day the Moon is a full circle
Krishna Paksha — the waning period of the Moon
Gibbous — less than half the Moon appears lit
questions.explanation: Shukla Paksha is waxing and Krishna Paksha is waning. Purnima is the full Moon day (not the invisible day), Amavasya is the new Moon day, and gibbous means MORE than half appears lit.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: A student fills Table 11.1 on the second and third mornings after a full Moon. Which entries should appear in the last two columns?
options: Bright portion: Increased; Moon–Sun separation: Farther
Bright portion: Decreased; Moon–Sun separation: Farther
Bright portion: Decreased; Moon–Sun separation: Closer
Bright portion: Increased; Moon–Sun separation: Closer
questions.explanation: After full Moon the Moon is waning, so the bright portion decreases each day, and at sunrise the Moon appears to move closer to the Sun in the sky day by day.

questions.topic: Phases of the Moon: Waxing and Waning
questions.question: Lunar eclipses are the main reason the Moon does not appear as a complete circle on most nights.
questions.explanation: False. Meera briefly wondered this, but eclipses are rare and brief. The Moon's changing appearance is due to its phases — how much of its lit half faces Earth.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: On a full Moon day, when the Sun is rising in the east, where is the Moon?
options: Directly overhead in the sky
Also rising in the east
Hidden below the horizon
Almost setting in the west
questions.explanation: On a full Moon day the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun in the sky, so as the Sun rises in the east the Moon is almost setting in the west.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: During the waning period, when the Moon's bright part has shrunk to a half circle, where is the Moon at sunrise?
options: Overhead
Setting in the west
Rising in the east
Close to the Sun
questions.explanation: The chapter states that when the bright part decreases to a half circle, the Moon is overhead at sunrise. Full Moon sets in the west at sunrise; the crescent is close to the Sun.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: At which time of day is a waxing Moon easiest to spot, according to the chapter?
options: At sunrise
At sunset
At midnight
At noon
questions.explanation: A waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset, while a waning Moon is easiest to spot at sunrise.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: By about how much does the time of moonrise change from one day to the next?
options: About 50 minutes earlier
About 24 hours later
About 50 minutes later
About 4 minutes later
questions.explanation: Moonrise happens about 50 minutes later each day because the Moon moves ahead in its orbit while Earth rotates, so Earth must turn a bit more for the Moon to appear.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: The chapter quotes moonrise at 14:23 on 7 April 2025 and at 15:17 on 8 April 2025. By how much did moonrise shift between the two days?
options: 54 minutes earlier
37 minutes later
94 minutes later
54 minutes later
questions.explanation: 15:17 minus 14:23 is 54 minutes, and it is later on the second day — consistent with the rule that the Moon rises roughly 50 minutes later each day.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: After the listed moonrise time, roughly how long may you need to wait before the Moon climbs high enough to be seen?
options: About 30 minutes
About 50 minutes
About 2 hours
About 5 minutes
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box says you may need to wait about 30 minutes past the listed moonrise time for the Moon to be high enough to see. The 50-minute figure is the daily delay in moonrise.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: The Moon always rises at exactly the moment the Sun sets.
questions.explanation: False. Many people believe this, but it is not true in general; moonrise shifts about 50 minutes later each day and can even happen in the afternoon.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: Because of its daily shift, the Moon always rises and sets at different times from the Sun.
questions.explanation: True. Since the Moon's position relative to the Sun changes from day to day, its rising and setting times differ from the Sun's.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: The newspaper lists moonrise at 3:00 p.m. today. Where and when could you spot the Moon?
options: In the western sky just before sunrise tomorrow
In the eastern sky during the afternoon daylight
Directly overhead at exactly 3:00 p.m. today
In the eastern sky only after the Sun has set
questions.explanation: A moonrise around 2:00–4:00 p.m. means the Moon climbs in the eastern sky during daylight, so it can be spotted in the afternoon. It will not be overhead at the moment it rises.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: On successive mornings after the full Moon, how does the Moon's position at sunrise change?
options: It appears farther from the Sun each day
It stays in the same place in the sky
It appears closer to the Sun each day
It swings between east and west daily
questions.explanation: As the bright part keeps decreasing after full Moon, the Moon appears to move closer to the Sun in the sky at sunrise — until, around new Moon, it is too close to the Sun to be seen.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: Which source does the chapter suggest for finding the moonrise time in your area?
options: The Bhuvan mapping platform run by ISRO's Cartosat programme
The Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics annual bulletin
The Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre launch schedule
The Positional Astronomy Centre website or a newspaper
questions.explanation: The chapter points to a local newspaper or the Positional Astronomy Centre (India Meteorological Department) website for moonrise times. Bhuvan is a mapping platform, not a moonrise service.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: Which TWO pieces of information help you decide where and when to look for the Moon on a given day?
options: The current phase of the Moon
The day of the week
Whether the Moon is waxing or waning
The date of the most recent lunar eclipse
The season of the year
questions.explanation: Knowing the phase and whether it is waxing or waning tells you roughly where the Moon is relative to the Sun and whether sunset or sunrise is the better time to look.

questions.topic: Locating the Moon in the Sky
questions.question: Around the 15th day of Activity 11.1, a student cannot find the Moon at either sunrise or sunset. What is the most likely explanation?
options: It is near new Moon: the Moon is close to the Sun, lit side facing away
It is near full Moon, so the Moon is too bright to see against the sky
The Moon has temporarily stopped revolving around the Earth
A lunar eclipse is hiding the Moon for the whole of that day
questions.explanation: About 15 days after full Moon comes new Moon: the Moon appears closest to the Sun in the sky and only its non-illuminated half faces Earth, so it cannot be seen. Eclipses are brief, and the Moon never stops revolving.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: Why does the Moon shine, according to the chapter?
options: It burns gases like a small star
It glows from heat trapped deep inside it
It reflects sunlight that falls on it
It reflects light from the Earth
questions.explanation: The Moon does not emit light of its own; it shines because it reflects sunlight that falls on it.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: At any moment, how much of the Moon's surface is lit by the Sun?
options: About a quarter of it
Almost all of it
Only a thin strip of it
About half of it
questions.explanation: The half of the Moon that faces the Sun receives sunlight and is illuminated; the other half stays non-illuminated. We see different amounts of that lit half from Earth.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: In Activity 11.2 (the ball-and-stick model), what represents the Earth?
options: The student's head
The soft ball on the stick
The torch or electric lamp
The dark open ground
questions.explanation: The ball represents the Moon, the torch or lamp represents the Sun, and the student's own head represents the Earth from which the Moon is viewed.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: In Activity 11.2 the ball is held towards the direction of the lamp (position E). Which real situation does this model?
options: Full Moon day
New Moon day
Gibbous phase
Half Moon day
questions.explanation: With the ball between you and the lamp you face its non-illuminated side and see no lit part — exactly like the new Moon. Holding it opposite the lamp (position A) models the full Moon.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: As the student turns slowly in the ball-and-lamp activity, what shape is the line separating the lit and unlit parts of the ball?
options: A straight vertical line
A jagged broken line
A curved line
A perfect circle
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the line separating the illuminated and non-illuminated portions appears curved, like the edge of the Moon's bright portion seen from Earth.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: In Fig. 11.5, at which positions of the Moon is MORE than half of its illuminated portion seen from Earth?
options: Positions D and F
Positions A and E
Positions C and G
Positions B and H
questions.explanation: At B and H we see more than half of the lit portion — the gibbous phase. D and F give the crescent (less than half); A is full, E is new; C and G show exactly half.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: Why do people in different parts of the Earth see nearly the same phase of the Moon on a given day?
options: The Moon stays fixed over one point of the Earth throughout the day
Earth's one-day rotation is much shorter than the Moon's month-long revolution
Sunlight reaches every part of the Earth at the same instant
The Moon's orbit is tilted slightly with respect to Earth's orbit
questions.explanation: Because Earth rotates once in a day while the Moon takes nearly a month to revolve, the Moon's position in its orbit barely changes during one day — so everyone sees nearly the same phase.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: Which statement about the Moon as seen from Earth is NOT correct?
options: Only one half of the Moon always faces the Earth
We can see only the illuminated portion of the Moon from Earth
The half of the Moon facing Earth is always its illuminated half
On new Moon day only the non-illuminated portion faces the Earth
questions.explanation: The same half always faces Earth, but that half is not always the lit half — the Sun lights whichever half faces it. The mismatch between the Earth-facing half and the Sun-facing half is what produces phases.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: The Moon's actual shape changes during the month, which is why we see different phases.
questions.explanation: False. The shape of the Moon itself does not change; only the portion of its illuminated half that we can see from Earth changes.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: On the new Moon day, only the non-illuminated half of the Moon faces the Earth.
questions.explanation: True. On new Moon day the Moon lies in the direction of the Sun, so the half facing Earth is the dark half and no lit portion is visible.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: In Fig. 11.5, the Moon moving from position A through C to E shows which phase sequence?
options: The waxing phase
A lunar eclipse
A solar eclipse
The waning phase
questions.explanation: From A (full) to C (half) to E (new) the visible lit part shrinks — the waning phase. From E through G back to A the Moon waxes.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: What does the chapter identify as the cause of the phases of the Moon?
options: A change in the fraction of the Moon's illuminated portion that is seen from Earth
A change in the amount of sunlight that reaches the Moon during the month
The Earth's shadow covering different amounts of the Moon on different days
A change in the Moon's distance from the Earth as it moves along its orbit
questions.explanation: Phases occur because, as the Moon revolves around Earth, different fractions of its lit half face us. The Sun always lights half of the Moon; Earth's shadow causes eclipses, not phases.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: In Activity 11.2, which TWO statements correctly describe the model?
options: The stick represents the axis of the Earth
The torch or electric lamp represents the Sun
The student's head represents the Sun
The soft ball represents the Moon
questions.explanation: The ball is the Moon, the lamp is the Sun and the student's head is the Earth. The stick is only a handle for holding the ball.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: In Fig. 11.5(a), on about which day of the cycle (counting the full Moon as Day 1) does the Moon reach position E, the new Moon?
options: Day 8
Day 15
Day 22
Day 26
questions.explanation: The figure labels A as Day 1 (full Moon), C as Day 8 (half), E as Day 15 (new Moon) and G as Day 22 (half again) — new Moon comes about two weeks after full Moon.

questions.topic: Why Phases Happen: The Ball-and-Lamp Model
questions.question: The question in the margin asks why the lit portion of the Moon seen from Earth decreases when the Moon appears closer to the Sun. Which answer fits the chapter's model?
options: Near the Sun's direction, the Moon receives much less sunlight
Near the Sun's direction, the Earth's shadow covers more of the Moon
Near the Sun's direction, the Moon moves farther away from Earth
Near the Sun's direction, mostly the Moon's dark half faces Earth
questions.explanation: When the Moon lies close to the Sun's direction (near position E), the half facing Earth is mostly the non-illuminated half, so only a thin lit crescent — or nothing — is seen. The Moon is still half-lit by the Sun.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: Why does the Moon take about 50 minutes longer than a day to return to nearly the same spot in the sky?
options: The Moon moves ahead in its orbit while Earth rotates, so Earth must turn a little more
The Moon slows down slightly each day while the Earth keeps rotating at the same rate
The Earth's rotation takes about 50 minutes longer than 24 hours every single day
Sunlight bends the Moon's path, shifting where it appears by about 50 minutes
questions.explanation: In one day Earth completes one rotation, but meanwhile the Moon has moved further along its orbit. Earth has to rotate some more for the Moon to appear in the same place — about 50 minutes more.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: In how much time does the Earth complete one rotation about its axis?
options: 29.5 days
24 hours
365 days
50 minutes
questions.explanation: The Earth rotates once about its axis in 24 hours (the mean solar day). 29.5 days is the Moon's phase cycle and 365 days is roughly a year.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: What is caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon?
options: The phases of the Moon
A solar eclipse
A lunar eclipse
The new Moon
questions.explanation: Earth's shadow on the Moon produces a lunar eclipse. Phases are NOT caused by Earth's shadow — that is a common misconception the chapter corrects.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: On which day of the lunar cycle can a lunar eclipse occur?
options: Only on a new Moon day
Only on a half Moon day
On any day of the cycle
Only on a full Moon day
questions.explanation: A lunar eclipse needs the Earth between the Sun and Moon, which happens only on a full Moon day. Solar eclipses can happen only on a new Moon day.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: If eclipses need a full or new Moon, why don't they happen every month?
options: The Moon's orbit is slightly tilted relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun
The Moon takes longer than a month to complete one full orbit of Earth
The Earth's shadow is usually too faint to be noticed on the Moon
The Sun, Moon and Earth are never in a straight line at any time
questions.explanation: Because of the small tilt of the Moon's orbit, on most full and new Moon days the Moon passes slightly above or below the line joining Sun and Earth. Eclipses occur only when the alignment is close.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: A solar eclipse can take place on a full Moon day.
questions.explanation: False. Solar eclipses happen only on new Moon days, when the Moon lies between the Earth and the Sun. Full Moon days are when lunar eclipses can occur.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: The Earth's shadow on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse, not the phases of the Moon.
questions.explanation: True. Phases arise from the changing orientation of Sun, Moon and Earth as the Moon revolves; Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: The Moon is exactly overhead at 9:00 p.m. tonight. At about what time will it be overhead tomorrow?
options: About 8:10 p.m.
About 9:50 p.m.
About 9:00 p.m.
About 10:40 p.m.
questions.explanation: Fig. 11.6 explains that after one rotation of Earth the Moon has moved on in its orbit, so Earth must rotate about 50 minutes more — the Moon is overhead about 50 minutes later, around 9:50 p.m.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: A seaside town records a high tide at 6:00 a.m. on Monday. Using the chapter's tide pattern, around when should a similar high tide occur on Tuesday?
options: Around 5:10 a.m.
Around 6:00 a.m.
Around 7:40 a.m.
Around 6:50 a.m.
questions.explanation: Tide levels are closely related to the Moon's position, and the Moon returns to the same position about 50 minutes later each day — so the similar tide comes around 6:50 a.m.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: Select the TWO correct statements about when eclipses can happen.
options: A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day
A lunar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day
A lunar eclipse can happen only on a full Moon day
A solar eclipse can happen during the crescent phase
questions.explanation: Lunar eclipses need Earth between Sun and Moon (full Moon); solar eclipses need the Moon between Sun and Earth (new Moon). Neither can occur during a crescent phase.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: An eclipse occurs on every full Moon day and on every new Moon day.
questions.explanation: False. The small tilt of the Moon's orbit means that on most full and new Moon days there is no eclipse; only positions where the orbits' planes cross are favourable for eclipses.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: Which observation best supports the idea that tides are linked to the Moon rather than to the Sun alone?
options: Tides repeat about 50 minutes later each day, matching the Moon's daily delay
Tides repeat at exactly the same clock time every day, like sunrise
Tides are highest at noon every day when the Sun is at its highest
Tides stop completely during the new Moon when the Moon is not seen
questions.explanation: The chapter points out that a similar tide recurs about 50 minutes later each day — the same delay the Moon shows — and that tide levels track the Moon's position and phase.

questions.topic: Moon's Orbit, Moonrise Delay, Eclipses and Tides
questions.question: In the chapter's Fig. 11.6 story, what has happened by the time Earth has completed one rotation after the Moon was overhead?
options: The Moon has completed exactly one full orbit around Earth
The Moon has revolved a bit further along its orbit
The Moon has returned to exactly the same overhead position
The Moon has moved to the opposite side of the Earth
questions.explanation: In one day the Moon moves only a small way along its roughly month-long orbit, so after Earth's full rotation the Moon is a bit ahead and Earth must rotate more to bring it overhead.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: The Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west every day. This apparent motion is primarily due to
options: the revolution of the Earth around the Sun
the revolution of the Moon around the Earth
the rotation of the Earth about its own axis
the movement of the Sun across the galaxy
questions.explanation: The daily apparent motion of the Sun is caused mainly by Earth spinning on its axis. Earth's revolution around the Sun gives the yearly cycle of seasons, not the daily cycle.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: What is the 'mean solar day'?
options: The average time between one sunrise in the east and the next sunset in the west
The average time for the Moon to return to the same position in the sky
The average number of daylight hours measured over a whole year
Average time from the Sun's highest point one day to its highest point the next
questions.explanation: The mean solar day is the average time the Sun takes to go from its highest position in the sky on one day to its highest position the next day — 24 hours.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: How can you tell when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky using a vertical stick?
options: The stick's shadow is shortest
The stick's shadow is longest
The stick casts no shadow at all
The shadow points towards the east
questions.explanation: The shadow cast by an object is shortest when the Sun is highest in the sky, so the time of the shortest shadow marks the Sun's highest position.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: In Activity 11.3, what is the recommended set-up and observing window?
options: A 1 m stick held at arm's length, marking its tip every hour from sunrise to sunset
A 1 m stick fixed vertically; shadow tip marked every minute from 11:00 a.m. to about 1:10 p.m.
A torch shone at a ball from 3 m, marking the lit edge every minute at night
A 1 m stick laid flat on the ground, marking its shadow every ten minutes till noon
questions.explanation: The activity fixes a 1 m stick vertically in sunlit ground and marks a dot at the tip of its shadow every minute from 11:00 a.m. until around 1:10 p.m. to catch the shortest shadow.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: Table 11.2 shows the shortest shadow at 12:20 on 23 March 2025 and at 12:19 on 24 March 2025. What duration of the solar day is recorded for 24 March?
options: 24 h 01 min
24 h 00 min
23 h 59 min
23 h 41 min
questions.explanation: From 12:20 on 23 March to 12:19 on 24 March is one minute short of 24 hours, i.e. 23:59 — which is what the table records.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: Why does Activity 11.3 ask you to mark a dot every minute rather than just once at noon?
options: So the stick's height can be measured more accurately
So the Sun's rising direction can be recorded for the day
So the length of the night can be estimated from the dots
So the time of the shortest shadow can be found by counting the dots
questions.explanation: You identify which dot is closest to the stick (the shortest shadow) and find its time by counting dots from 11:00 a.m. Marking only at clock noon would miss the true highest point, which the table shows was at about 12:20.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: What does Table 11.2 reveal about the time of the Sun's highest point on 22–24 March 2025?
options: It was around 12:20, not at 12:00 noon by the clock
It was exactly at 12:00 noon on all three days
It shifted by about 50 minutes from day to day
It occurred at sunrise on each of the three days
questions.explanation: The recorded shortest shadows were at 12:20, 12:20 and 12:19 — close to, but not exactly, clock noon, and nearly the same each day (giving a day of about 24 hours).

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: In Activity 11.3 the stick's shadow is longest when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky.
questions.explanation: False. The shadow is SHORTEST when the Sun is highest; it is longest near sunrise and sunset when the Sun is low.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: The mean solar day is 24 hours long.
questions.explanation: True. The average time between successive highest positions of the Sun is 24 hours, and Table 11.2 gives values of about 24:00 and 23:59.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: In Activity 11.3, which quantity is kept fixed and which is observed to change?
options: The shadow's length is fixed; the stick's height changes
The stick's height is fixed; the shadow's length changes
The time of day is fixed; the stick's position changes
The Sun's position is fixed; the ground's slope changes
questions.explanation: The vertical 1 m stick is the fixed set-up; what varies through the day — and what you track with the dots — is the length (and direction) of its shadow as the Sun moves across the sky.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: Which TWO items are needed to carry out Activity 11.3 as described?
options: Binoculars for viewing the Sun safely
A torch and a small soft ball on a stick
A 1 m stick fixed vertically in flat sunlit ground
Observations made at sunrise and sunset
Dots marked at the shadow tip every minute from 11:00 a.m. to about 1:10 p.m.
questions.explanation: The day-measuring activity uses a vertical 1 m stick and minute-by-minute marks around midday. The torch and ball belong to the phases activity, and sunrise/sunset viewing belongs to Activity 11.1.

questions.topic: The Day and the Mean Solar Day
questions.question: A student repeats Activity 11.3 but marks dots only from 12:30 p.m. to 1:10 p.m. Based on Table 11.2, what is the likely problem?
options: The shadow will be too short to mark during that interval
The dots will be too close together to count accurately
The Sun will have already set before the first dot is made
The shortest shadow (about 12:20) will have been missed entirely
questions.explanation: The table shows the shortest shadow around 12:19–12:20, so starting at 12:30 means the Sun's highest point has already passed and the activity cannot find solar noon.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: About how long does the Moon take to go through all its phases?
options: About 29.5 days
About 24 hours
About 354 days
About 365.25 days
questions.explanation: The Moon's cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days — nearly a month — which is the basis of the month as a unit of time.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: How long does the Earth take to complete one revolution around the Sun?
options: Exactly 365 days
Nearly 365¼ days
About 354 days
About 12 lunar months
questions.explanation: The Earth takes nearly 365¼ days to revolve once around the Sun, during which it passes through one cycle of seasons — defining a solar year. 354 days is a lunar year.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: What observation in ancient times led to lunar calendars with 12 months?
options: Exactly 12 full Moons occur in every calendar year without fail
The Moon's phases repeat 12 times during a single solar day
Twelve different constellations rise at sunset through the year
Nearly 12 cycles of the Moon's phases fit into one cycle of seasons
questions.explanation: People noticed that about 12 cycles of lunar phases fit within one cycle of seasons, giving lunar calendars a day, a month of about 29.5 days, and a year of 12 lunar months.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: Why do the seasons not stay matched to the same months in a purely lunar calendar?
options: The lunar year is 354 days while the seasons repeat in about 365 days
The lunar year is 365 days while the seasons repeat in about 354 days
The Moon's phases become irregular during the winter months
The Earth's rotation speeds up and slows down with the seasons
questions.explanation: Twelve lunar months make 354 days, about 11 days short of the ~365-day cycle of seasons, so each lunar year the months slip earlier relative to the seasons.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: Twelve lunar months of about 29.5 days each add up to approximately how many days?
options: 365 days
354 days
336 days
360 days
questions.explanation: 12 × 29.5 = 354 days — the length of a lunar year, as the chapter states.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: By about how many days does a lunar year fall short of a solar year?
options: About 29.5 days
About 1 day
About 11 days
About 20 minutes
questions.explanation: The 12 lunar months add up to 354 days, nearly 11 days less than the ~365-day solar year. (20 minutes is the sidereal–tropical year difference; 1 day in 4 years is the leap-day correction.)

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: In a purely lunar calendar, the same lunar month always falls in the same season year after year.
questions.explanation: False. Because the lunar year (354 days) is shorter than the cycle of seasons (~365 days), the months drift through the seasons over the years.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: The phases of the Moon provide a natural cycle longer than a day and form the basis of the month.
questions.explanation: True. The roughly 29.5-day phase cycle is the natural cycle on which the month is based.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: Match each unit of time to the periodic phenomenon it is based on.
options: Day — Moon's phase cycle; Month — Earth's rotation; Year — cycle of seasons
Day — Earth's rotation; Month — cycle of seasons; Year — Moon's phase cycle
Day — cycle of tides; Month — Earth's revolution; Year — Moon's revolution
Day — Earth's rotation; Month — Moon's phase cycle; Year — cycle of seasons
questions.explanation: The day comes from the Sun's daily return to its highest point (Earth's rotation), the month from the Moon's ~29.5-day phase cycle (its revolution around Earth), and the year from the cycle of seasons (Earth's revolution around the Sun).

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: Amol was born on 6 May on a full Moon day. Will his birthday fall on a full Moon every year?
options: No — the Gregorian calendar is solar, so the Moon's 29.5-day cycle does not repeat on the same date
Yes — the Moon's phases always repeat on the same Gregorian date every year
Yes — 6 May is always a full Moon because 12 lunar months equal a solar year
No — the full Moon can occur only in the winter months of the Gregorian calendar
questions.explanation: The Gregorian calendar follows the Sun (365/366 days) while 12 lunar cycles take only 354 days, so the phase on any given date shifts by about 11 days each year. 6 May will be a full Moon only occasionally.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: A total of 37 full Moons occur during 3 years of a solar calendar. Which reasoning shows that at least two of them must fall in the same calendar month?
options: A lunar month is 29.5 days, so every month must contain exactly one full Moon
Three years contain only 36 months, so 37 full Moons cannot each have a different month
Three years contain 36 months, so exactly one month must have had no full Moon
A solar year has 365 days, so there must be 13 full Moons in each year
questions.explanation: There are 3 × 12 = 36 months in three years but 37 full Moons. Since 37 objects placed in 36 boxes force at least one box to hold two, some month must have two full Moons.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: Can two full Moons occur within the same Gregorian month? Choose the best answer.
options: No, because the phase cycle is always longer than any Gregorian month
No, because full Moons occur only once every 30 days exactly
Yes — the 29.5-day phase cycle is shorter than a 30- or 31-day month
Yes, but only in February, which has fewer than 29.5 days
questions.explanation: A 29.5-day cycle fits inside a 30- or 31-day month, so a full Moon on the 1st can be followed by another on the 30th or 31st. February (28/29 days) is the one month that can never hold two.

questions.topic: Month, Year and Lunar Calendars
questions.question: Which TWO statements about lunar calendars are correct?
options: A lunar year is 365 days long
A lunar year consists of 12 lunar months
The day is not a unit in lunar calendars
A lunar month is close to 29.5 days long
Lunar months are always 30 days long
questions.explanation: Lunar calendars have the day as the shortest unit, months of nearly 29.5 days, and a 354-day year of 12 lunar months.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: The Gregorian calendar, widely used today, is an example of a
options: lunar calendar
luni-solar calendar
sidereal calendar
solar calendar
questions.explanation: The Gregorian calendar is a solar calendar based on the tropical year; it adjusts month lengths to add up to 365 days (366 in leap years).

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: What need led people to create solar calendars?
options: Knowing when seasons arrive, for agriculture
Tracking the exact date of each full Moon
Fixing festival dates by the lunar phase
Predicting the dates of solar eclipses
questions.explanation: It was important to know the arrival of seasons for agricultural purposes, so a year synchronised with the seasons — a solar calendar — was needed.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Why do Gregorian months have 30 or 31 days and February only 28?
options: Each month must match one cycle of the Moon's phases
The months are adjusted so they add up to 365 days
The months are adjusted so they add up to 354 days
Each month must begin on the day after a new Moon
questions.explanation: In solar calendars the month lengths are adjusted to total 365 days; that is why some months have 30 days, others 31 and February 28.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Why is a leap day added every four years?
options: The lunar year falls short of the solar year by about one day
The Earth's rotation slows by one day every four years
Each year's extra quarter day adds up to about a day in four years
The seasons shift by one full day every four years
questions.explanation: Beyond 365 days, Earth takes nearly an extra quarter day to complete its revolution. Over four years these extra hours add up to roughly one day, which is added as 29 February.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Using the rules in the chapter, which of these years WAS a leap year?
questions.explanation: Century years skip the leap year (1700, 1800, 1900) but every 400 years it is added back — 1600 and 2000 were leap years.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Which of these years was NOT a leap year under the Gregorian rules described?
questions.explanation: 1900 is divisible by 4 but, being a century year not divisible by 400, its leap day was skipped. 1600 and 2000 were added back as leap years, and 2024 is an ordinary year divisible by four.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Why are leap years skipped in most century years such as 1700, 1800 and 1900?
options: Adding a day every four years slightly under-corrects, since the year is a bit more than 365¼ days
Adding a day every four years slightly over-corrects, since the year is a bit less than 365¼ days
Century years are deliberately shortened to make up for the lunar year's 11-day shortfall
The Moon's orbit tilts more in century years, so a leap day would cause extra eclipses
questions.explanation: Earth takes slightly LESS than 365¼ days between spring equinoxes, so a leap day every four years adds a little too much. Skipping it every 100 years (and restoring it every 400) keeps the calendar aligned.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: What is the 'tropical year'?
options: The time for the same stars to rise again at sunset
The time for the Moon to complete twelve phase cycles
The time between two successive spring equinoxes
The time between two successive summer solstices only
questions.explanation: The time between successive spring equinoxes is the tropical year; the Gregorian calendar is based on it. The star-based period is the sidereal year.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: How does the sidereal year compare with the tropical year?
options: It is shorter by about 20 minutes
It is longer by about 11 days
It is exactly the same length
It is longer by about 20 minutes
questions.explanation: The sidereal year (time for the same stars to rise again at sunset) is longer than the tropical year by a mere 20 minutes, so differences between the two kinds of calendar take a long time to show.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Which statement about leap years is NOT correct?
options: In every leap year the extra day is added to the month of March
In a leap year February has 29 days instead of 28
A Gregorian year divisible by four normally gets a leap day
Leap days keep the calendar synchronised with the seasons
questions.explanation: The leap day is 29 February, not a day in March. The Indian National Calendar adds its leap day to Chaitra, which does start in March — but the Gregorian leap day is in February.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: The sidereal year is shorter than the tropical year by about 20 minutes.
questions.explanation: False. It is the other way round: the sidereal year is LONGER than the tropical year by about 20 minutes.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Modern astronomers use the sidereal year to keep track of the Earth's position in its orbit around the Sun.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter notes that in modern times astronomers use the sidereal year for tracking Earth's orbital position, while the Gregorian calendar follows the tropical year.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: If we stopped having leap years, in approximately how many years would Indian Independence Day (15 August) fall in winter?
options: About 180 years
About 700 years
About 70 years
About 4 years
questions.explanation: Without leap days the calendar slips about 1 day every 4 years. To move 15 August about half a year (~180 days) into winter takes 180 × 4 ≈ 720, i.e. roughly 700 years.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: If leap years were abolished, by roughly how many days would the calendar drift from the seasons in 100 years?
options: About 100 days
About 1 day
About 25 days
About 11 days
questions.explanation: The uncorrected quarter day per year accumulates to one day every four years, so in 100 years the drift would be about 100 ÷ 4 = 25 days.

questions.topic: Solar Calendars and Leap Years
questions.question: Which TWO statements about the Gregorian calendar are correct?
options: All of its months have exactly 30 days
A year divisible by four normally gets an extra day in February
It adds an intercalary month every two to three years
It is based on the tropical year
questions.explanation: The Gregorian calendar is a solar calendar based on the tropical year, with a leap day in February in years divisible by four (with century-year exceptions). Intercalary months belong to luni-solar calendars.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: A luni-solar calendar primarily counts days and months by the Moon's phases but also
options: adds a leap day to the month of February every four years
begins every year on the day after the spring equinox
fixes every one of its months at exactly 30 or 31 days
makes adjustments to stay in step with the cycle of seasons
questions.explanation: Luni-solar calendars use the Moon's phases for months yet add corrections (an extra month every few years) to remain synchronised with the seasons.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: What is 'Adhika Maasa'?
options: An extra (intercalary) month added every few years
An extra day added to Chaitra in a leap year
The dark fortnight ending on the new Moon
The month in which Diwali is celebrated
questions.explanation: Adhika Maasa is the intercalary month inserted every 2–3 years in luni-solar calendars to make up the accumulated gap between 12 lunar months and the solar year.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: Why is an extra month needed roughly every 2–3 years in luni-solar calendars?
options: The Moon's phase cycle gets longer by 11 days every two to three years
The yearly 11-day shortfall of lunar months accumulates to nearly a month
The seasons arrive 11 days later each year because of Earth's wobble
The Moon completes an extra orbit around the Earth every third year
questions.explanation: Twelve lunar months (354 days) fall about 11 days short of the solar year each year; after 2–3 years the difference is close to a full month, which is then added back.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: If 12 lunar months fall about 11 days short of the solar year, roughly how much have they fallen behind after 3 years?
options: About 11 days — less than half a month
About 66 days — more than two months
About 33 days — close to one lunar month
About 3 days — a negligible amount
questions.explanation: 3 × 11 = 33 days, which is a little more than one lunar month of 29.5 days. This is why the intercalary month comes about every 2–3 years.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the Indian luni-solar month names listed in the chapter?
options: Jyeshtha
Bhadrapada
Margashirsha
Ramazan
questions.explanation: The chapter lists Chaitra, Vaisakha, Jyeshtha, Ashadha, Shravana, Bhadrapada, Ashwin, Kartika, Margashirsha, Pausha, Magha and Phalguna. Ramazan is the month at whose end Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated — a different calendar.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: In an 'Amant' calendar, when does a month begin and end?
options: Begins the day after new Moon and ends on the new Moon
Begins the day after full Moon and ends on the full Moon
Begins on the spring equinox and ends on the next equinox
Begins on 22 March and ends thirty days later
questions.explanation: Amant months run from the day after a new Moon to the next new Moon. Purnimant months run from the day after a full Moon to the next full Moon.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: In a 'Purnimant' calendar, on which day does the month end?
options: On the new Moon day
On the full Moon day
On the half Moon day
On the spring equinox
questions.explanation: Purnimant (from Purnima, full Moon) months end on the full Moon and start the day after it; Amant months end on the new Moon (Amavasya).

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: In Amant calendars the month ends on the day of the full Moon.
questions.explanation: False. Amant months end on the new Moon (Amavasya); it is Purnimant months that end on the full Moon.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: Luni-solar calendars, which combine lunar months with solar-year corrections, are used in many parts of India.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter says such calendars combine elements of both solar and lunar calendars and are used in many parts of India.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: Scientific studies show the Moon is moving farther from Earth and revolving more slowly. How would this affect the need for intercalary months in luni-solar calendars?
options: Needed more often, since longer lunar months make the lunar year overshoot the solar year
Needed more often, since a slower Moon means more new Moons in each solar year
Needed less often, since longer lunar months bring 12 of them closer to a solar year
No change, because intercalary months depend only on the Earth's rotation
questions.explanation: A slower revolution means a longer phase cycle, so 12 lunar months add up to more than 354 days and the yearly shortfall shrinks below 11 days. It would take longer to accumulate a full month, so the extra month is needed less often.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: Which name is given as an alternative for the month Margashirsha in the list of Indian luni-solar months?
options: Bhadrapada
Phalguna
Shravana
Agrahayan
questions.explanation: The chapter lists 'Margashirsha (or Agrahayan)' among the twelve month names.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: Which TWO features define a luni-solar calendar?
options: A leap day is added to February
An extra month is added every few years to stay in step with the seasons
The year always begins on 22 March
Every month has exactly 30 or 31 days
Months are counted by the Moon's phases
questions.explanation: Luni-solar calendars combine lunar months with a periodic intercalary month to track the seasons. Fixed 30/31-day months and February leap days belong to solar calendars; 22 March is the Indian National Calendar's new year.

questions.topic: Luni-solar Calendars and Indian Months
questions.question: A calendar used in a community adds an extra month roughly every two to three years. Which type of calendar is it?
options: Luni-solar
Purely lunar
Purely solar
Sidereal solar
questions.explanation: Only luni-solar calendars add an intercalary month. Purely lunar calendars make no seasonal correction, and solar calendars correct with a leap day, not a month.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: The Indian National Calendar is a
options: lunar calendar of 354 days
solar calendar of 365 days
luni-solar calendar with Adhika Maasa
sidereal calendar of 12 lunar months
questions.explanation: The Indian National Calendar is a solar calendar consisting of 365 days in a year (366 in leap years), used alongside the Gregorian calendar for official purposes.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: On which date does the Indian National Calendar year begin in a regular year, and why that date?
options: 21 March — the day of the spring equinox
21 June — the day of the summer solstice
22 March — the day after the spring equinox
1 January — matching the Gregorian new year
questions.explanation: The year begins on 22 March, the day after the spring equinox. In leap years the new year falls on 21 March because a day is added to Chaitra.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: In a regular year of the Indian National Calendar, which months have 31 days?
options: The first to fifth months
Every alternate month
Only the last six months
The second to sixth months
questions.explanation: In a regular year the second to sixth months have 31 days and the rest have 30 days — five 31-day months and seven 30-day months, totalling 365.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: Check the arithmetic: in a regular year of the Indian National Calendar there are five 31-day months and seven 30-day months. Does this give the stated total?
questions.explanation: Months 2–6 (five months) have 31 days and the other seven have 30: 155 + 210 = 365, exactly the length of a regular solar year.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: How is a leap year handled in the Indian National Calendar?
options: A day is added to Phalguna and the year starts on 23 March
A day is added to Chaitra and the year starts on 21 March
An extra month, Adhika Maasa, is inserted into the year
February of the Gregorian calendar is given 29 days instead
questions.explanation: Leap years are matched to the Gregorian calendar by adding a day to Chaitra, the first month. In such years the new year begins on 21 March instead of 22 March.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: Which is the first month of the Indian National Calendar?
options: Vaisakha
Kartika
Chaitra
Phalguna
questions.explanation: Chaitra is the first month (beginning 22 March in a regular year); Vaisakha is the second. Fig. 11.9 shows Chaitra of Shaka Era 1947 running 22 March – 20 April 2025.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: Fig. 11.9 shows Vaisakha running from 21 April to 21 May 2025. How many days is this, and does it fit the chapter's rule?
options: 30 days; it fits, since the 2nd to 6th months have 30 days
31 days; it does not fit, since only Chaitra has 31 days
30 days; it does not fit, since Vaisakha should have 31 days
31 days; it fits, since the 2nd to 6th months have 31 days
questions.explanation: 21 April to 21 May inclusive is 31 days (10 days left in April + 21 in May). Vaisakha is the second month, and the rule says months 2–6 have 31 days, so it fits.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: When was the Indian National Calendar recommended by the Calendar Reform Committee adopted for use?
options: 21 March 1956 CE, i.e. 1 Chaitra 1878 Saka
22 March 1952 CE, i.e. 1 Chaitra 1874 Saka
15 August 1947 CE, i.e. 1 Chaitra 1869 Saka
1 January 1950 CE, i.e. 1 Chaitra 1872 Saka
questions.explanation: The CRC was set up in 1952 and its 'Unified National Calendar' was adopted with effect from 21 March 1956 CE, which was 1 Chaitra 1878 Saka.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: Shaka year 1947 began on 22 March 2025, and 1 Chaitra 1878 Saka was 21 March 1956. What is the difference between the Shaka and Gregorian year numbers?
options: 68 years
78 years
88 years
57 years
questions.explanation: 2025 − 1947 = 78 and 1956 − 1878 = 78: both data points agree that the Shaka era runs 78 years behind the Gregorian count.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: Who chaired the Calendar Reform Committee set up by the Government of India in 1952?
options: Vikram Sarabhai
C. V. Raman
Meghnad Saha
Homi Bhabha
questions.explanation: Meghnad Saha, the astrophysicist famous for the Saha equation, was the chairperson of the Calendar Reform Committee. Vikram Sarabhai is the Father of the Indian Space Programme.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: The Indian National Calendar follows the general principles of which ancient text?
options: Taittiriya Samhita
Rashtriya Panchang
Rigveda Samhita
Surya Siddhanta
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the Indian National Calendar follows the general principles of the Surya Siddhanta. The Taittiriya Samhita is quoted on Uttarayan/Dakshinayan, and the Rashtriya Panchang is a modern yearly publication.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: In the Indian National Calendar the leap day is added to the last month of the year.
questions.explanation: False. The leap day is added to Chaitra, the FIRST month, which is why the leap-year new year begins on 21 March.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: The Indian National Calendar is used along with the Gregorian calendar for several official purposes.
questions.explanation: True. The Government of India uses the national calendar alongside the Gregorian calendar for multiple official purposes.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: Which statement about the Indian National Calendar is NOT correct?
options: Some of its months have 28 days
Its month names come from traditional Indian calendars
Its months have either 30 or 31 days
It consists of 365 days in a regular year
questions.explanation: Unlike the Gregorian calendar, where February has 28 days, Indian National Calendar months have only 30 or 31 days. The other statements are all given in the chapter.

questions.topic: Indian National Calendar and Calendar Reform
questions.question: Which TWO statements about Meghnad Saha are correct?
options: He founded the Indian Space Research Organisation
He developed the Saha equation while studying stars and their temperatures
He is known as the Father of the Indian Space Programme
He chaired the Calendar Reform Committee
questions.explanation: Saha was a pioneering astrophysicist (Saha equation; the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics in Kolkata is named after him) and chaired the CRC. The space-programme achievements belong to Vikram Sarabhai.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: On which days does the Sun rise exactly in the east and set exactly in the west?
options: On the solstices
On full Moon days
On the equinoxes
On new Moon days
questions.explanation: The figure in 'Our scientific heritage' shows the Sun rising exactly in the East and setting exactly in the West on the equinoxes; on solstices it rises farthest north or south of east.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: In which direction of due east does the Sun rise in summer and in winter, according to the chapter?
options: A little south of east in summer; a little north of east in winter
Exactly east in summer; a little north of east in winter
A little north of east in both summer and winter
A little north of east in summer; a little south of east in winter
questions.explanation: Careful observation shows the Sun rises slightly northward of east in summer and slightly southward of east in winter, with the extremes at the solstices around 21 June and 21 December.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: What is 'Uttarayan'?
options: The Sun's apparent northward movement from December to June
The Sun's apparent southward movement from June to December
The Moon's northward movement during Shukla Paksha
The six months during which the Sun rises exactly in the east
questions.explanation: Uttarayan is the Sun's apparent northward movement (of its rising point) from December to June; the southward movement from June to December is Dakshinayan.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: The Taittiriya Samhita verse 6.5.3 quoted in the chapter says, in effect, that
options: the Moon waxes for six months and wanes for six months
the Sun moves south for six months and north for six months
the year has twelve months of thirty days each
the Sun rises exactly in the east throughout the year
questions.explanation: The verse is translated: 'Thus the Sun moves southwards for six months and northwards for six months' — the Dakshinayan and Uttarayan cycle.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: According to the Surya Siddhanta as described in the chapter, which constellation was in the background of the Sun around the winter solstice in ancient times?
options: Cancer (Karka)
Sagittarius (Dhanu)
Capricorn (Makar)
Aries (Mesha)
questions.explanation: Ancient Indian texts noted that Capricorn (called Makar) was in the Sun's background around the winter solstice; entering Capricorn began the six months of Uttarayana, while entering Cancer began Dakshinayana.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: How did ancient people work out that the year is about 365 days long, even without knowing that Earth revolves around the Sun?
options: By measuring the Earth's speed along its orbit with early telescopes
By counting exactly twelve full Moons in every cycle of seasons
By timing how long the Moon's shadow took to cross the Earth
Through years of careful sky-watching, noticing repeating patterns and cycles
questions.explanation: People in ancient times lacked modern instruments and did not know Earth revolves around the Sun, yet by patiently observing natural cycles they determined the year's length to be about 365 days.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: On 15 September, in which direction is the Sun's rising point drifting from day to day?
options: Southward, because it is in the Dakshinayan period
Northward, because it is in the Uttarayan period
It is not moving, because it is near an equinox
Eastward, because it is close to the winter solstice
questions.explanation: Dakshinayan is the Sun's apparent southward movement from June to December, so in September the sunrise point is moving southward (even though it is near due east around the equinox, it is still drifting).

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: Ancient Indian astronomers knew that the Earth revolves around the Sun and used that knowledge to build their calendars.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter says people in ancient times did NOT know Earth revolves around the Sun; they built calendars from observed patterns and cycles in the sky.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: In the past, the equinoxes and solstices were tracked by identifying the stars that rose at sunset.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter says equinoxes and solstices were tracked by noting which stars rose at sunset, as recorded in texts like the Surya Siddhanta.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: Which statement about the Sun's rising point is NOT correct?
options: The Sun rises farthest north of east around 21 June
The Sun rises exactly in the east on every day of the year
The Sun rises farthest south of east around 21 December
The Sun rises exactly in the east on the equinoxes
questions.explanation: The Sun rises exactly in the east only on the equinoxes; through the year its rising point swings north (summer) and south (winter), reaching extremes at the solstices.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: According to the Surya Siddhanta quotation, from what moment do the six months of Uttarayana begin?
options: The Sun's entrance into the constellation of Cancer
The first full Moon after the spring equinox
The Sun's entrance into the constellation of Capricorn
The day on which the Sun rises exactly in the east
questions.explanation: The verse says that from the Sun's entrance into Capricorn six months make up its northward progress (Uttarayana), and from its entrance into Cancer six months make up Dakshinayana.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: Select the TWO correct statements about the Sun's rising position.
options: Around 21 June the Sun rises farthest north of east
Uttarayan is the Sun's movement from June to December
Around 21 December the Sun rises farthest south of east
On the equinoxes the Sun rises farthest north of east
questions.explanation: The solstices (about 21 June and 21 December) mark the northern and southern extremes of sunrise. On equinoxes the Sun rises due east, and Uttarayan runs from December to June.

questions.topic: Uttarayan, Dakshinayan and Scientific Heritage
questions.question: A student sketches the eastern horizon and marks the sunrise point on the first of every month for a year. What pattern does the chapter lead us to expect?
options: The point stays fixed at due east throughout the whole year
The point drifts steadily northward every month without ever returning
The point swings north from June to December and south from December to June
It swings north from December to June and back south from June to December
questions.explanation: This is the Uttarayan/Dakshinayan cycle: sunrise moves northward from the December solstice to the June solstice and southward again, repeating every year in step with the seasons.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: On which day of the Indian calendar is Diwali celebrated?
options: The new Moon of Kartika
The full Moon of Kartika
The full Moon of Phalguna
The tenth day of Ashwina
questions.explanation: Diwali falls on the new Moon of Kartika. Holi is on the full Moon of Phalguna, and Dussehra on the tenth day of Ashwina.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Which festival is celebrated on the full Moon of Vaisakha?
options: Makar Sankranti
Buddha Purnima
Eid-ul-Fitr
Dussehra
questions.explanation: Buddha Purnima is on the full Moon of Vaisakha; Holi is on the full Moon of Phalguna, Diwali on the new Moon of Kartika and Dussehra on the tenth day of Ashwina.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Why do most Indian festivals fall on different Gregorian dates in successive years?
options: They are fixed to the solstices, which move each year
They follow the Gregorian calendar's leap-year corrections
They follow lunar or luni-solar calendars tied to the Moon's phases
They are set each year by the Calendar Reform Committee
questions.explanation: Many festivals are tied to phases of the Moon and hence to lunar or luni-solar calendars, whose months do not line up with the solar Gregorian calendar — so the dates shift.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: How does the year-to-year shift of a luni-solar festival such as Diwali differ from that of a purely lunar festival such as Eid-ul-Fitr?
options: Diwali can move through different months; Eid shifts by less than a month
Both festivals always stay within the same Gregorian month every year
Both festivals move about 11 days later in the Gregorian calendar each year
Diwali shifts by less than a month; Eid can move through different months over the years
questions.explanation: Luni-solar calendars add an intercalary month every few years, keeping their festivals within about a month. Purely lunar calendars make no such correction, so Eid-ul-Fitr drifts about 11 days earlier each year and can fall in any month.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: By about how many days does the Gregorian date of Eid-ul-Fitr move each year, and in which direction?
options: About 11 days earlier
About 11 days later
About 1 day earlier
About 29.5 days later
questions.explanation: Because the lunar year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, a purely lunar festival like Eid-ul-Fitr falls about 11 days earlier in the Gregorian calendar each year.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Which group of festivals follows a solar sidereal calendar and so falls on almost the same Gregorian date every year?
options: Diwali, Holi, Buddha Purnima, Dussehra and Eid-ul-Fitr
Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Bihu, Vaisakhi and Puthandu
Diwali, Pongal, Holi, Vaisakhi and Buddha Purnima
Eid-ul-Fitr, Bihu, Dussehra, Puthandu and Holi
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box lists Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Bihu, Vaisakhi, Poila Baisakh and Puthandu as festivals on a solar sidereal calendar; the Moon-based festivals shift dates.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Why do sidereal-calendar festivals like Makar Sankranti slowly drift away from the solstice they were once tied to?
options: Leap years are skipped every 100 years in the Gregorian calendar
The Moon's orbit around Earth is tilted and gradually shifts the dates
A slow wobble of Earth's axis makes sidereal and tropical years differ slightly
The lunar year is 11 days shorter than the solar year each year
questions.explanation: The slow wobble of Earth's axis (like a wobbling top) creates the small difference between sidereal and tropical years, so dates on the sidereal calendar move ahead in the tropical (Gregorian) calendar.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Makar Sankranti moves ahead by one day every 71 years. By roughly how much would it shift in 710 years?
options: About 71 days
About 1 day
About 100 days
About 10 days
questions.explanation: 710 ÷ 71 = 10, so the festival would move ahead by about 10 days in 710 years.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: What is the 'Rashtriya Panchang'?
options: An annual publication of celestial positions, used to fix festival dates
A list of luni-solar month names used in the Indian National Calendar
A website that gives daily moonrise times for every Indian city
The Calendar Reform Committee's 1956 report on a unified calendar
questions.explanation: The Positional Astronomy Center publishes the Rashtriya Panchang each year — detailed calculations of positions of the Moon, Sun etc. for a central location in India — and gives advance intimation of festival dates to the Government.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Why can the date of a festival differ by a day between eastern and western India in the same year?
options: Eastern India follows a solar calendar while western India follows a lunar one
Dates depend on the exact lunar phase at sunrise, and sunrise is earlier in the east
The Moon rises about 50 minutes earlier in western India than in eastern India
Western India adds the intercalary month a year later than eastern India
questions.explanation: Many festival dates are based on the exact lunar phase at sunrise. Since sunrise occurs earlier in eastern India than in western India, the phase at sunrise can differ, shifting the date by a day — hence the need for a uniform Rashtriya Panchang.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Which of these is a raga whose name reflects Moon imagery, according to the chapter?
options: Chandrakala
Ardhachandran
Chandrakauns
Madhubani
questions.explanation: Chandrakauns, Chandranandan and Shubhapantuvarali are ragas named with Moon imagery. Chandrakala and Ardhachandran are Bharatanatyam mudras, and Madhubani is a painting style.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Holi is celebrated on the new Moon of the month of Phalguna.
questions.explanation: False. Holi falls on the FULL Moon of Phalguna; it is Diwali that is celebrated on a new Moon (of Kartika).

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Eid-ul-Fitr can occur in different months of the Gregorian calendar in different years.
questions.explanation: True. Eid-ul-Fitr follows a purely lunar calendar that does not correct for the 11-day yearly shortfall, so over the years it moves through all the Gregorian months.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: Which TWO festivals follow a solar sidereal calendar?
options: Diwali
Pongal
Holi
Bihu
Eid-ul-Fitr
questions.explanation: Pongal and Bihu (with Makar Sankranti, Vaisakhi, Poila Baisakh and Puthandu) follow a solar sidereal calendar. Diwali and Holi follow luni-solar calendars and Eid-ul-Fitr a lunar one.

questions.topic: Festivals and Astronomical Phenomena
questions.question: A festival fell on 10 April one year, 30 March the next year, and then jumped to 18 April the year after. Which calendar does it most likely follow?
options: Purely lunar — it moves about 11 days earlier every single year
Solar tropical — it stays within a few days of the same date
Solar sidereal — it moves one day ahead every 71 years
Luni-solar — the jump shows an intercalary month was added
questions.explanation: Moving 11 days earlier and then leaping forward is the signature of a luni-solar calendar: the lunar months slip earlier until an Adhika Maasa pushes the festival back later in the Gregorian year.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: What is the Moon described as in relation to the Earth?
options: Earth's artificial satellite
Earth's natural satellite
A planet orbiting the Sun
A star reflecting Earth's light
questions.explanation: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite, orbiting our planet; man-made satellites launched from Earth are artificial satellites.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: At about what height do most artificial satellites orbit, and how long does one orbit take?
options: About 80 km, taking roughly 24 hours
About 8000 km, taking roughly 10 minutes
About 800 km, taking roughly 100 minutes
About 800 km, taking roughly 29.5 days
questions.explanation: Most artificial satellites orbit about 800 km above Earth's surface and complete one orbit in roughly 100 minutes.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: If a satellite takes about 100 minutes per orbit, roughly how many orbits does it complete in one day?
options: About 24
About 10
About 100
About 14
questions.explanation: A day has 1440 minutes; 1440 ÷ 100 ≈ 14.4, so the satellite completes about 14 orbits each day.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: Which set lists purposes of artificial satellites given in the chapter?
options: Communication, navigation, weather monitoring, disaster management and scientific research
Mining the Moon, cooling the atmosphere, generating tides and lighting the night sky
Communication, replacing the Moon's light, changing seasons and controlling eclipses
Navigation, controlling moonrise times, measuring the solar day and tracking tides
questions.explanation: The chapter says satellites help in communication, navigation, weather monitoring, disaster management and scientific research.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: What do ISRO's Cartosat satellites do?
options: Observe stars and other celestial objects for scientific study
Capture high-quality Earth images for maps, city planning and disasters
Study the Sun from a point between the Earth and the Sun
Carry small student-built satellites into orbit around the Moon
questions.explanation: Cartosat satellites image the Earth to improve maps, plan cities and handle natural disasters; the Bhuvan platform uses these images. AstroSat observes stars; Aditya L1 studies the Sun.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: Which ISRO mission makes scientific observations of stars and other celestial objects?
options: Cartosat
Aditya L1
AstroSat
Mangalyaan
questions.explanation: AstroSat observes stars and celestial objects. Cartosat images the Earth, Aditya L1 studies the Sun and Mangalyaan went to Mars.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: Which of these is a small satellite built and launched by Indian students with ISRO's help?
options: AzaadiSat
AstroSat
Cartosat
Aditya L1
questions.explanation: ISRO lets Indian students build and launch small satellites such as AzaadiSat, InspireSat-1 and Jugnu. AstroSat, Cartosat and Aditya L1 are ISRO's own missions.

questions.topic: Artificial Satellites and ISRO
questions.question: According to Activity 11.4, when and how can you spot an artificial satellite?
options: Only at midnight, as a slow-moving bright disc like the Moon
Just before sunrise or after sunset, as a fast-moving point of light
At midday, as a dark spot crossing the face of the Sun
Only during a lunar eclipse, as a flash near the Moon's edge
questions.explanation: Satellites appear as points of light with steady or flickering brightness moving very fast across the sky, best looked for just before sunrise or after sunset, with the naked eye or binoculars.
